label: Yirmeyahu (Jeremiah) — Part 7 — Chapters 49–52
summary_plain: YHWH pronounces judgment on the nations: Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Qedar, Chatsor, Elam, and above all — Babylon. Two full chapters (50-51) declare Babylon's destruction: She who sits on many waters, rich in treasures — her end has come. Babylon was a golden cup in YHWH's hand, making all the earth drunk. YHWH says: I am against you, O destroying mountain — hammer of the whole earth. Flee from the midst of Babylon — let every one save his life. Chapter 52 recounts the fall of Yerushalayim — the siege, the breach, the burning of the Temple, the exile — confirming everything Yirmeyahu prophesied.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Jeremiah manuscripts (4QJer-a through 4QJer-e) and the Orit Ge'ez. Chapters 50-51 constitute the longest single oracle against a foreign power in the prophetic literature — two chapters devoted to Babylon's judgment. The imagery is dense and multi-layered: Babylon as golden cup (51:7), as dwelling on many waters (51:13), as hammer of the whole earth (50:23), as destroying mountain (51:25). These images are reused in Revelation 17-18 almost verbatim — the whore of Babylon sitting on many waters, the golden cup, the call to flee. Chapter 52 is nearly identical to 2 Melakhim 25 — a historical appendix confirming the prophetic word. The DSS fragments and the LXX confirm significant textual variants in the Babylon oracles.

key_terms.definition: Yirmeyahu 49:7-22 pronounces judgment on Edom; the proud Edomites who live in the clefts of the rock and whose wisdom is renowned will be brought down; YHWH will make Edom a desolation.
Yirmeyahu 50-51 is the longest oracle in the book — a sustained declaration of Babylon's fall: the city will be uninhabited forever; the nations will plunder it; YHWH will vindicate his people.
Yirmeyahu 51:6 — 'Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of YHWH's vengeance.'
Yirmeyahu gave a scroll of Babylon's judgment to Serayahu to read when he reached Babylon, then tie a stone to it and throw it in the Euphrates: 'So shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.'

Yirmeyahu 52 is an almost verbatim parallel to 2 Melakhim 25, recording the fall of Yerushalayim, the exile, the numbers of the exiled, and the Temple vessels taken — the documented historical outcome of Yirmeyahu's prophecies.

The book ends with King Yehoyakhin, imprisoned in Babylon for 37 years, being released by Evil-Merodach king of Babylon; he ate regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life — a sign of hope at the book's end.

Yirmeyahu 52 catalogs the bronze pillars Yakhin and Boaz, the sea, the stands, and the vessels of the Temple taken to Babylon; this detailed inventory documents the full extent of the material destruction.

Nebuchadnezzar killed Tzidkiyahu's sons before his eyes at Riblah, then had Tzidkiyahu's eyes gouged out; the last thing Tzidkiyahu saw was the execution of his sons — fulfilling Yirmeyahu's prophecy.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, broke down all the walls of Yerushalayim; the city's physical defenses were completely demolished to prevent future resistance.

The Babylonian captain of the guard who carried out the destruction of Yerushalayim after the city fell; he burned the Temple, the palace, and all the great houses; he exiled the people and left only the poorest to work the land.

faq.question: What is the significance of the Babylon oracles in Yirmeyahu 50-51?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 50-51 is the longest oracle against a single target in the book. Its theological core: Babylon, which YHWH used as his instrument to judge Yisra'el, will itself be judged for what it did. YHWH is not simply Babylon's employer — Babylon exceeded its mandate with excessive cruelty. YHWH will now send Medes against Babylon as he sent Babylon against Yehudah.

faq.question: Why is the scroll-thrown-in-Euphrates sign in Yirmeyahu 51 so powerful?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu gave Serayahu a written scroll of all Babylon's coming judgment. After reading it at Babylon, Serayahu was to tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates with the declaration: 'So shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.' The act performs the prophecy: the city's fate is as sure as the weighted scroll sinking — the word goes into the place itself.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of Yehoyakhin's release at the end of Yirmeyahu 52?
faq.answer: The book ends not with judgment but with a small act of grace: after 37 years in prison, Yehoyakhin is released, given a seat above other captive kings, and fed regularly at the Babylonian king's table. This is not the full restoration — it is a flicker of hope. The Davidic line is alive; a descendant sits at a foreign king's table. The story is not over.

faq.question: What does Yirmeyahu 52's catalog of exiles and Temple vessels document?
faq.answer: The historical appendix in Yirmeyahu 52 carefully counts three deportations (3,023; then 832; then 745 — total 4,600) and inventories the Temple's bronze objects. This serves as documentation that the exile was real, numbered, and partial — not a complete erasure. The specific numbers argue against total destruction and preserve the community's historical memory for restoration.

faq.question: What is the oracle against Edom in Yirmeyahu 49 about?
faq.answer: Edom was condemned for pride — trusting in the inaccessibility of its rock fortresses (Petra, in the clefts of the rock) and its famous wisdom traditions. YHWH declares no rock is inaccessible to him. Edom's pride deceived it. The oracle in Yirmeyahu 49 overlaps thematically with Ovadyahu (Obadiah) and Yesha'yahu 34, all targeting Edom's self-sufficiency.

faq.question: What does 'flee from Babylon' mean in Yirmeyahu 51?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 51:6, 45 commands the exiles in Babylon to flee when YHWH's time of judgment on Babylon arrives. This does not contradict Yirmeyahu 29's earlier 'seek the peace of the city' — that instruction was for the present exile period; the 'flee' is for the future day of Babylon's fall. The timing matters: settle during the exile; leave when the judgment time comes.

faq.question: Why is Babylon called a golden cup in YHWH's hand in Yirmeyahu 51:7?
faq.answer: The image in Yirmeyahu 51:7 is striking: Babylon was YHWH's instrument for pouring out judgment on the nations — a golden cup that made the whole earth drunk with the wine of YHWH's wrath. But the cup itself will now be shattered. The nations who drank from it will now mourn Babylon's fall. YHWH is the one who wielded Babylon, not Babylon's own gods.

faq.question: What is the significance of the Redeemer (Go'el) language in Yirmeyahu 50:34?
faq.answer: YHWH is called Yisra'el and Yehudah's Go'el — kinsman-redeemer — in Yirmeyahu 50:34. The Go'el is the family member who steps in to redeem a relative from bondage, poverty, or death (the institution underlying Ruth's story). By using this language for the return from Babylon, Yirmeyahu frames YHWH's restoration as a family rescue, not merely a political act.

faq.question: How does the fall of Yerushalayim in Yirmeyahu 52 fulfill the specific prophecy of Tzidkiyahu's fate?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu had prophesied to Tzidkiyahu that he would be brought before Nebuchadnezzar and his eyes would see the king of Babylon (Yirmeyahu 34:3). The fulfillment in chapter 52 is precisely calibrated: Nebuchadnezzar killed Tzidkiyahu's sons before his eyes at Riblah, then had his eyes put out. The last thing Tzidkiyahu's eyes saw was the execution of his sons — Yirmeyahu's prophecy was fulfilled to the letter.

faq.question: What nations are covered in Yirmeyahu's oracles in chapters 49-51?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 49-51 covers: Ammon (49:1-6), Edom (49:7-22), Damascus (49:23-27), Qedar and Khatsor (49:28-33), Elam (49:34-39), and then the extended Babylon oracle (chapters 50-51). Together with chapters 46-48 (Mitzrayim, Plishtim, Moav), these form the most comprehensive set of national oracles in any single prophetic book.

faq.question: Why does Yirmeyahu end with a note of hope rather than judgment?
faq.answer: The book's final verses (52:31-34) recording Yehoyakhin's release from prison serve as the book's last word: even after total disaster, YHWH's covenant purposes are not exhausted. The Davidic line survived in Babylon. The 70-year exile Yirmeyahu predicted is in progress. The New Covenant promises of chapters 30-33 are still ahead. The final note of Yehoyakhin eating at the king's table is deliberate: survival is real, and the story continues.
